FINAL DETERMINATION
The Indiana Board of Tax Review ("Board") having reviewed the facts and evidence, and having
considered the issues, now finds, and concludes the following:
I. INTRODUCTION
1. 7202 East (Indianapolis) Tanford LLC brought appeals (1) challenging the 2021 and
2022 assessments for its three Indianapolis hotels, and (2) alleging a lack of uniformity
and equality in assessments within the hotels' competitive market. •B ecause the totality of
the evidence did not suffice to demonstrate the true tax value for any ofTanford's hotels,
we must apply the value presumptions specified under Indiana Code§ 6-l.1-15-20(t).
And because Tanford did not demonstrate the true tax value for its properties or any

III. OBJECTIONS
7. The Assessor objected to all of Tanford's exhibits on grounds that they were not
authenticated and contained inadmissible hearsay. He also argued that Tanford failed to
lay a foundation for the exhibits, which we construe as simply reiterating his first two
7202 East (Indianapolis) Tanford LLC
Final Determination
Page 3 of 17

grounds.2 Tanford responded that the information in the exhibits came from Costar and
public records, although it did not offer testimony from a sworn witness to support that
claim~ The ALJ took the objections under advisement.
8. We overrule the objections. Our acµninistrative law judges "regulate the course of the
proceedings without recourse to the rules of evidence:'' 52 Ind. Admin. Code 4-6-9(a).
A party's failure to authenticate a document therefore does not necessarily require us to
exclude it. But it dqes affect the weight we give to the document.
9. Similarly, although the Indiana Rules of Evidence make hearsay generally inadmissible
(Ind. Evidence Rule 802),. we may admit hearsay. 52 I.A.C. 4-6-9(d). But we cannot
base our final determination solely on hearsay that has been properly objected to unless it
falls within a recognized exception to the hearsay rule. Id.
10. Tanford's exhibits are hearsay: they contain out-of-hearing assertions offered to prove the
truth of the matters asserted, such as income, expenses, and occupancy rates for
Tanford's hotels; unattributed value conclusions based on capitalizing the hotels' net•
operating income ("NOI"); and data concerning the physical characteristics of various
other hotels. See Ind. Evidence Rule 801(c) (defining hearsay). Tanford did not lay a
foundation to show that the documents fall within any recognized exception to the
hearsay rule. At best, it offered Amato' s unsworn statement that some of the information
was gathered from public records. That is far from sufficient to lay a foundation for
admission under the exceptions for records of a regularly conducted activity or public
records. See Evid. R 803(6), (8).
11. Thus, while we admit the exhibits over Tanford's hearsay objection, we can11ot base our
determination solely on the hearsay contained within those exhibits. As explained below,
we do not rely on Tanford's exhibits in reaching our final determination.

V. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
A. We must initially presume that each property's 2021 assessment equaled its true tax
value.
31. Generally, a taxpayer has the burden of proof when challenging a property tax
assessment. Accordingly, the assessment on appeal, "as last determined by an assessing
official or county board," will be presumed to equal "the property's true tax value" unless
and until rebutted by evidence from the parties. Ind. Code § 6-1.1-15-20( a) (e ff. March
21, 2022). Where the totality of the evidence does not suffice to determine the property's
true tax value, the presumption holds. LC. § 6-1.1-15-20(±).
32. However, the burden of proof shifts if the property's assessment represents an increase of
more than 5% over its last-determined assessment for the prior tax year. LC. § 6-l.1-l 5-
20(b) . Subject to certain exceptions that do not apply here, the assessment "is no longer
presumed to be equal to the property's true tax value, and the assessing official has the
burden of proof." Id
33. If the burden has shifted, and "the totality of the evidence presented to the [Board] is
insufficient to determine the property's true tax value[,] ... then the property's prior year
assessment is presumed to equal the property's true tax value." LC. § 6-1.1-15-20(±).
Tanford conceded it had the burden of proof in its 2021 appeals, and we must initially
presume that each property's 2021 assessment equals its true tax value for that year.
7202 East (Indianapolis) Tanford LLC

B. Because the totality of the evidence is insufficient to determine the value for any of
Tanford's properties, we must presume that each property's 2021 assessment equals its
true tax value for that year.
34. We are the trier of fact in property tax appeals, and our charge is to "weigh the evidence
and decide the true tax value of the property as compelled by the totality of the probative
evidence" before us. LC.§ 6-1.1-15-20(±). Our conclusion "may be higher or lower than
the assessment or the value proposed by a party or witness." Id Regardless of which
party has the burden of proof, either party "may present evidence of the true tax value of
the property, seeking to decrease or increase the assessment." LC. § 6-1 J-15-20(e ) .
. 35. True tax value does not mean "fair market value" or "the value of the property to the
user." LC. § 6-1.1-31-6( c) . Instead, itis determined under the rules of the Department of
Local Government Finance ("DLOF"). LC. §§ 6-l.1-3 l-5(a) -6(f). Formost real
pror,erty types, the DLGF defines true tax value as "market value-in-use," which it in turn
defines as "[t]he market value-in-use of a property for its current use, as reflected by the
utility received by the owner or by a similar user, from the property." 2021 REAL
PROPERTY ASSESSMENT MANUAL at 2.
36. To meet its burden of proof, a party "must present objectively verifiable, market-based
evidence" of the property's value .. Piotrowski v. Shelby Cnty. Ass 'r, 177 N.E.3d 127, 132
(Ind. Tax Ct. 2021) (citation omitted). Neither the taxpayer nor the assessor may rely on
the mass appraisal "methodology" of the "assessment regulations." PIA Builders & Dev.,
LLC v. Jennings Cnty. Ass 'r, 842 N.E.2d 899, 900 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2006). This is because
the "formalistic application" of the procedures and schedules from the DLGF's
assessment guidelines lacks the market-based evidence necessary to establish a specific
property's market value-in-use. Piotrowski, 177 N.E.3d at 133.
37. Market-based evidence may include "sales data, appraisals, or other information
compiled in accordance with generally accepted appraisal principles;" Peters v.
Garojfolo, 32 N.E.3d 847, 849 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2015). Relevant assessments are also
admissible, but arguments that "another property is 'similar' or 'comparable' simply
7202 East (Indianapolis) Tanford LLC

because it is on the same street are nothing more than conclusions ... [and] do not
constitute probative evidence." Marinov v. Tippecanoe Cnty. Ass'r, 119 N.E.3d 1152,
1156 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2019). Finally, the evidence must reliably indicate the property's .
value as of the valuation date. O'Donnell v. Dep't ofL oe. Gov't Fin., 854N.E.2d 90, 95
(Ind. Tax Ct. 2006). The valuation date is January 1 of each assessment year. I.C. § 6-
1.1-2-1.S(a}; 50 I.A;C. 27-5-2.
38. . These appeals present a difficult valuation question. We are concerned solely with the
true tax value ofTanford's real property. But hotels normally sell as going concerns,
including FF &E and intangible property. THE APPRAISAL INSTITUTE, THE APPRAISAL OF
. REAL ESTATE 663-64. (15th ed. 2020).4 And "establislnng a reasonable allocation of the
value opinion among the realty and non-realty components can be challenging." Id. at
664; see also Chesapeake Hotel, LP v. Saddlebrook Twp., 22 N.J, Tax 525, 527-30 (N.J.
Tax Ct. 2005) ( outlining disagreement between nationally recognized appraisers over
how to isolate the contributory value of real property in appraising hotels under the
income capitalization approach).
39. None of the value opinions or analyses offered by the parties even attempts to explain
whether, or how, they allocated the value ofTanford's properties between realty and non
realty components. For that reason alone, the parties' evidence was insufficient to
determine the true tax value for any of Tanford's properties.
40. There are more reasons why the evidence does not suffice to demonstrate the true tax
value for Tanford's properties. We begin with Tanford's evidence. Before addressing
the methodological failings of the analyses Tanford offered, we highlight'a more
fundamentaLproblem: there is no evidence to show who prepared the analyses or the
sources from which the underlying data was obtained, much less that the data was
accurate.

41. In any case, the analyses are methodologically flawed. Tanford first offered a valuation
for each property using the income capitalization approach, which estimates a property's
present value through dividing its expected NOi by a market-supported capitalization
rate. Lacy Diversified Indus., Ltd. v. Dep't ofL oe. Gev't Fin., 799 N.E.2d 1215, 1224
(Ind. Tax Ct.2003) (citations omitted). To provide a sound value indication under that
approach, "one must not only examine the historical and current income, expenses, and
occupancy rates for the subject property, but the income, expenses and occupancy rates
of comparable properties in the market as well." Indiana MHC, LLC v. Scott Cnty. Ass 'r,
987 N.E.2d 1182, 1185-1186 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2013) (citation omitted); see also, Southlake
Ind, LLC v. Lake_ Cnty. Ass 135 N.E.3d 692, 696 (Ind. Tax Ct2019) review denied
tr
("[W]hen valuing a property under the income approach, the fee simple interest in the
property must be valued based on an estimate of market rent, not contract rent.").
Similarly, the capitalization rate "generally reflects the annual rate of return necessary to
attract investment capital." Lacy Diversified, Indus., Ltd. v. Dep 't ofL oe. Gov 't Fin., 799
N.E.2d at 1224 (citations omitted).
42. It is unclear whether the NOi from Tanford's analyses is hased on the properties' historic
income and expenses as opposed to market-level income and expenses. And the analyses
do not indicate how the chosen capitalization rates were derived, much less that they
reflected the -annual rate of return necessary to attract investment capital. Tanford
therefore failed to show that the analyses comply with generally accepted appraisal
principles._
43. Tanford's sales-comparison analyses are similarly unreliable. They do little to compare
Tanford's properties to any of the purportedly comparable hotels in terms of
characteristics that affect market value. And they do not even attemptto explain how
relevant differences affected the properties' relative values. The analyses therefore fail to
comply with generally accepted appraisal principles, and the raw sales data does not
suffice to demonstrate the true tax value for any of Tanford's properties. See Long v.

Wayne Twp. Ass.'r, 821 N.E.2d 466, 470-71 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2005) (hold.ing that taxpayers'

44. Tetrick's sales-comparison analyses do not fare any better. She offered more data about
the features of her purportedly comparable hotels than Tanford offered in its analyses .
... But like Tanford, Tetrick did not even attempt to explain how any relevant differences
affected the properties' relative values. And eventhough Tetrick used sales from before

45. In addition, Co Star's description of the Hyatt Place transaction as a "1031 Exchange,
Auction Sale" should have prompted Tetrick to investigate whether the reported sale
price needed to be adjusted. Like-kind exchanges under section 1031 of the Internal
Revenue Code can be complex, with higher-than-normal transaction costs. APPRAISAL OF
REAL EST ATE at 3 83. And buyers may pay more in those transactions because they lose
the ability to defer taxes if they do not meet the code's timing requirements, which would
necessitate an adjustment. Id. Yet there is nothing to indicate that Tetrick explored
whether an adjustment to the Hyatt Place sale was necessary.
46. The Assessor also offered CoStar graphs showing hotel sale prices over time. While
those graphs might show changes in market conditions for the markets or submarkets in
which Tanford's properties compete, they do little or nothing to demonstrate the value of
those specific properties.

C. The Assessor had the burden of proof for 2022, and the lack of probative valuation
evidence requires us to presume that each property's true tax value is equal to its
assessment from the prior year.
48. For 2022, each property's assessment increased by more than 5% over its 2021
assessment-Marriott by 8.75%; Fairfield by_8.43%; and Delta by 8.89%. Thus, the
Assessor had the burden of proof. If the totality of the evidence does not suffice to
demonstrate the properties' true tax values, we must presume their values are equal to
their 2021 assessments. LC. § 6-1.1-15-20 (b ), (f).
49. The parties relied on the same evidence and analyses for Tanford's 2022 appeals as they
did for 2021. For the reasons we have already explained that evidence does not suffice to
demonstrate the properties' true tax values. We musttherefore presume that the 2021
assessments equal the properties' true tax values for 2022.
D. Tanford did not prove it was entitled to relief based on a lack of uniformity and
equality in assessments.
50. Finally, Tanford argued that it was making an "equity" claim in addition to its claims
contesting the accuracy of its assessments. Tanford did not explain the legal
underpinnings for its equity claim, but it pointed to its assessment-comparison analysis
and argued that its hotels were assessed for higher unit prices than their competition. We
understand Tanford to be claiming that it is entitled to relief under our state constitution's
property taxation clause based on a lack of uniformity and equality in assessment. See
IND. CONST. ART. 10 § l(a) (requiring the Indiana General Assembly to "provide by law
for a uniform rate of assessment and taxation"). Indiana Code § 6-1.1-15-20 does not
apply to such challenges, and Tanford had the burden of proving its claim by a
preponderance of the evidence. See Thorsness v. Porter Cnty. Ass 'r, 3 N.E.3d 49, 52
(Ind. Tax Ct. 2014) (holding that predecessor to LC.§ 6-1.1-15-20 did not apply to claims
alleging a lack of uniformity and equality); see also, LC.§ 6-1.1-15-40) (providing that
our findings must be based on a pr~ponderance of the evidence).

51. Tanford failed to meet its burden. Under the property taxation clause, taxpayers are
entitled to a uniform rate of assessment, which is measured against the external
benchmark of market value-in-use. Westfield GolfP ractice Ctr., LLC v. Washington·
Twp. As§'r, 859 N.E.2d 396, 399 (Ind. Tax Ct. 2007). •T anfotd, however, did not
demonstrate the market value-in-use for its properties or for any of the purportedly
comparable properties it claims were more favorably assessed. It therefore failed to
prove its properties were assessed and taxed at a different rate than other properties. See
Westfield Golf, 859 N.E2d at 399 (holding that taxpayer failed to prove its assessment
violated the property taxation clause where it did not show the market value-in-use for its
property or for any comparable properties).
VI. CONCLUSION
52. Tanford bore the burden of proof for the 2021 assessment year. Because the totality of
the evidence did not suffice to demonstrate the properties' true tax values, we must
presume their assessments are equal to their values for that year. We therefore order no
change to the 2021 assessments. But the Assessor had the burden of proof for the 2022 •
assessment year. He failed to.meet his burden, and the totality of the evidence was again
insufficient to determine the properties' values. In accordance with LC. § 6-1. l-15-20(f),
we therefore order that the 2022 assessments be changed to match the 2021 values.
Finalli, we find that Tanford failed to prove it was entitled to any relief based on an
alleged lack of uniformity and equality in assessments.
